stem:
Tatenda placed 600 day-old broiler chicks (mean mass 0.04 kg) near Chinhoyi. Deaths each week were:

| Week | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Deaths | 18 | 6 | 3 | 2 | 2 | 1 |

The survivors were sold live at six weeks with a mean mass of 2.3 kg at US\$4.20 each (assume this price). The batch ate 2,180 kg of feed. Variable costs were: chicks US\$450, feed US\$1,199, vaccines and medicines US\$60, litter, fuel and other US\$96. A sample bird of 2.3 kg gave a dressed carcass of 1.702 kg.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Name **one** viral disease against which broilers are vaccinated.
parts.explanation: Newcastle disease or Gumboro (infectious bursal) disease.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the mortality percentage for the batch, to one decimal place.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the feed conversion ratio of the batch, to two decimal places.
parts.explanation: Gain = 568 × 2.3 − 600 × 0.04 = 1,306.4 − 24 = 1,282.4 kg; FCR = 2,180 ÷ 1,282.4 = 1.70. Ignoring the chicks' starting mass gives 1.67.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Calculate the dressing percentage of the sample bird.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Calculate the gross margin for the batch, in US\$.
parts.explanation: Income = 568 × 4.20 = US\$2385.60; costs = 450 + 1,199 + 60 + 96 = US\$1,805; gross margin = US\$580.60. Using all 600 chicks for income ignores the deaths.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Income = 568 × 4.20 = US\$2385.60; costs = 450 + 1,199 + 60 + 96 = US\$1,805; gross margin = US\$580.60. Using all 600 chicks for income ignores the deaths.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Most deaths occurred in week 1. Suggest and explain **three** possible causes.

points.description: Brooder too cold (or draughts), so chicks crowded, chilled or were smothered.
Chicks did not find feed and water quickly (drinkers/feeders too far or empty), so they dehydrated or starved.
Weak or infected chicks from the hatchery / poor hygiene in a house not cleaned and rested.

parts.explanation: Brooding, feed and water, chick quality and hygiene.

parts.label: (g)
parts.stem: Describe and explain how Tatenda should manage his next batch of broilers from before the chicks arrive until they are sold, so that fewer die and they grow well.

points.description: Clean, disinfect and rest the house for about two weeks; fresh dry litter 5-10 cm; footbath; rat-proofing (breaks disease cycles).
Pre-heat the brooder and set up the chick guard, feeders and drinkers before arrival.
Brood at about 32-35 °C at chick level, reducing about 3 °C a week, adjusting to chick behaviour (crowding = cold, spread and panting = hot).
Ventilate without draughts using curtains; keep litter dry to prevent coccidiosis.
Feed starter, then grower and finisher, with clean water always; raise feeders and drinkers to back height to cut waste.
Vaccinate against Newcastle and Gumboro disease on schedule; remove dead birds; restrict visitors (all-in, all-out).
Keep records of deaths, feed and weekly weights to spot problems and calculate FCR.
Withdraw feed 8-12 h before sale/slaughter; sell at the planned age when demand is high.

explanation: Broiler batch performance (mortality, FCR, dressing percentage, gross margin) and a reasoned management plan.
hints: Gain = survivors × final mass − chicks × 0.04 kg.
For the long part, follow the batch from before the chicks arrive to sale.

stem:
Rudo keeps 800 commercial layers in a deep-litter house near Marondera. The table shows how the laying percentage changed with the age of the flock.

| Age of flock (weeks) | 20 | 24 | 28 | 40 | 56 | 72 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Hen-day laying (%) | 12 | 78 | 92 | 88 | 80 | 64 |

In June (30 days) the 800 hens laid 20,640 eggs and each hen ate about 0.12 kg of layer mash a day.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: From the table, at about what age did the flock reach peak production?

options.rationale: At 20 weeks the flock had only just started laying (12%).

options.content: 72 weeks, when the hens were oldest and most experienced at laying
options.rationale: Production was lowest of the laying ages (64%).

parts.explanation: Production rises steeply after point of lay, peaks at 28 weeks and then falls slowly.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the hen-day laying percentage for June.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: How many trays of 30 eggs were filled in June?

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Calculate the mass of feed used per dozen eggs in June, in kg, to two decimal places.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: State **two** signs Rudo would use to pick out non-laying hens for culling.

points.description: Small, pale, shrunken comb and wattles.
Small, dry, puckered vent / pelvic bones close together (about one finger) / yellow colour returning to shanks.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Explain why the lights in the layer house are kept on to give about 16 hours of light a day.

points.description: Long days stimulate the hen's hormones that control egg production.
A shorter or falling day length reduces laying, so light is kept long and never reduced during lay.

parts.label: (g)
parts.stem: Suggest why the flock should be replaced at about 72 weeks of age.

points.description: Laying has fallen to 64%, so feed per dozen eggs rises and each hen earns less than she costs.
Off-layers can be sold for meat and the house cleaned and restocked with point-of-lay pullets.

parts.explanation: Economics of the end of lay.

parts.label: (h)
parts.stem: Describe and explain how Rudo should manage her layers to keep egg production and egg quality high.

points.description: House: dry, deep litter; good ventilation without draughts; correct stocking density; nest boxes (about one per 4-5 hens) in a dim area; perches.
Feed layer mash high in calcium (plus shell grit) from point of lay, with clean water always; avoid sudden feed changes.
Light: about 16 hours a day, never reduced during lay.
Collect eggs at least two or three times a day to keep them clean and reduce breakage and egg eating.
Do not wash eggs; candle, grade and pack broad end up; store cool.
Health: vaccinate (e.g. Newcastle disease), control mites and worms, footbath, keep out visitors and wild birds.
Keep daily egg, feed and death records to detect problems early.
Cull non-layers regularly and replace the flock at the end of lay.

parts.explanation: Housing, feeding, light, egg handling, health, records and culling, each with a reason.

explanation: Layer production curve, laying percentage, feed efficiency and a management plan for high egg output.
hints: Feed per dozen = total feed ÷ dozens of eggs.
For the long part, cover housing, feeding, lighting, eggs and health.

stem:
Breeding records from a piggery near Harare.

| Sow | Date served | Piglets born alive | Piglets weaned |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Sow A | 2 June 2026 | 11 | 10 |
| Sow B | 20 June 2026 | 12 | 9 |
| Sow C | 9 July 2026 | 10 | 9 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: State the expected farrowing date of sow B, using a gestation of 114 days.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the total number of piglets weaned.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage of piglets born alive that died before weaning, to one decimal place.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: The piglets are weaned at 42 days and the sows are served 5 days after weaning. Calculate the number of litters per sow per year, to two decimal places.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Why are the piglets given an iron injection at about three days old?

options.content: To protect them against African swine fever
options.rationale: There is no iron 'vaccine'; iron prevents anaemia.

options.content: Sow's milk is low in iron and piglets on concrete cannot get it from soil
To strengthen their teeth before they are clipped
options.rationale: Teeth are clipped on day 1; iron is for blood.

options.content: To make them gain fat quickly so that they can be sold as porkers at weaning
options.rationale: Iron prevents anaemia; it is not a fattening treatment.

parts.explanation: Iron is needed for haemoglobin; piglets grow fast with small iron stores.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: State **two** signs that a sow is about to farrow.

points.description: Nest building (biting and arranging bedding) / restlessness.
Swollen vulva / milk can be squeezed from the teats.

parts.label: (g)
parts.stem: Explain how a farrowing crate with a creep area reduces piglet deaths.

points.description: The crate makes the sow lie down slowly, so piglets can move away and are not crushed.
The heated creep area keeps piglets warm and away from the sow, preventing chilling.

parts.label: (h)
parts.stem: Describe and explain the care of piglets from birth until weaning.

points.description: At birth: clear mucus from nose and mouth; dry the piglet; cut and dip the navel in iodine (prevents infection).
Ensure every piglet suckles colostrum within hours (antibodies, energy); help weak piglets to a teat / foster extras.
Day 1: clip needle teeth (prevents injury to littermates and the sow's teats).
About day 3: iron injection (prevents anaemia).
Identify by ear notching/tattoo; castrate males not for breeding within the first two weeks (less stress).
Keep them warm in the creep area and protect from crushing with a farrowing crate or rails; clean, dry pen against scours.
Offer creep feed and clean water from about 1-2 weeks, so they grow and are ready for weaning.
Wean at about 4-8 weeks (here 6 weeks): move the sow out, leave piglets in their pen, change feed gradually; deworm.

parts.explanation: Ordered piglet care with ages and reasons.

explanation: Sow records: farrowing date, piglet losses and litters per year; care of piglets to weaning.
hints: Litters per year = 365 ÷ (gestation + lactation + days to service).
For the long part, work from birth to weaning, with ages and reasons.

stem:
A rancher near Masvingo weighed a group of beef cows on veld every two months.

| Month | November | January | March | May | July | September |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Mean cow mass (kg) | 380 | 410 | 440 | 445 | 420 | 395 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: During which period did the cows gain mass?

options.rationale: The cows lost mass in the dry season.
Correct: the rainy season, when grazing is green.

options.content: The whole year, because the mass at the end was higher than in July
options.rationale: September (395 kg) is lower than May (445 kg).

parts.explanation: Mass rose from 380 to 445 kg in the rains, then fell to 395 kg in the dry season.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the mass lost per cow from May to September, in kg.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate this loss as a percentage of the May mass, to one decimal place.
parts.explanation: 50 ÷ 445 × 100 = 11.2%. Dividing by the September mass gives 12.7%.
parts.workedSolution: 1. 50 ÷ 445 × 100 = 11.2%. Dividing by the September mass gives 12.7%.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain why the cows lost mass between May and September.

points.description: In the dry season the veld grass is dry, scarce and low in protein (and phosphorus).
Rumen microbes digest the poor grass slowly, so the cows eat less and use body reserves.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Name the lick that prevents cattle chewing bones and catching botulism.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Assume one bull to 30 cows. How many bulls are needed for 150 cows?

parts.label: (g)
parts.stem: Using the data, explain why the rancher plans for calves to be born from October to December.

points.description: Calves are born near the start of the rains, when the veld turns green.
Cows are then gaining mass and have good feed to produce milk, so calves grow well and cows recover condition to conceive again.

parts.explanation: Match calving to the feed supply.

parts.label: (h)
parts.stem: State **two** methods of identifying beef cattle.

points.description: Branding (hot-iron or freeze).
Ear tags / ear notches / tattoos.

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: Describe and explain the management practices the rancher should carry out in the herd during one year.

points.description: Breeding season of about three months with about one bull to 25-30 cows, timed for calving at the start of the rains; pregnancy test and cull open cows.
Supervise calving; ensure colostrum and navel care; identify calves (ear tags, branding).
Disbud and castrate young calves early (less stress, safer handling, docile steers).
Dip or spray against ticks (often weekly in the wet season) to prevent tick-borne diseases.
Dose against worms at strategic times and vaccinate (e.g. anthrax, blackleg, lumpy skin disease, botulism) on veterinary advice.
Dry-season supplements: protein/urea licks, phosphate lick and salt, hay or stover, to limit mass loss.
Wean calves at about 6-8 months so cows regain condition; sell weaners or finish them.
Keep stocking within carrying capacity, rotate paddocks and keep herd records (births, weights, treatments, sales).

explanation: Seasonal mass change of beef cows on veld and the year's management of a beef herd.
hints: Dry-season grass is low in protein and phosphorus.
